# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. # `updates/` — the flows that move a repo between versions

Canon-internal machinery (never vendored, like [`vendoring/`](../vendoring/README.md)): one runner
per **flow**, each moving a repo from the versions it has installed to the ones this canon tree
ships. The design — why the corpus splits into a versioned engine and versioned packs, and what
each flow may and may not do — is [`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md`](../docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md);
the release discipline the engine's versions follow is [`engine/RELEASES.md`](../engine/RELEASES.md).

| File | Flow |
|---|---|
| [`engine-update.mjs`](engine-update.mjs) | The **engine update**: replace the mount's engine wholesale, run the engine migrations in the repo's gap, converge the non-workflow wiring, stamp the new version, and gate the merge on the converged tree's own `selftest --strict`. Deterministic end to end — no agentic stage, and no lane to add one. |
| [`pack-update.mjs`](pack-update.mjs) | The **pack update**: the same shape, per declared pack — replace the pack's tree, run its records, stamp its version, same gate. It enforces `minEngineVersion` against the version the TARGET runs, it may write `.github/workflows/` (which the engine flow may not), and it ends by saying whether the agentic apply stage is needed. |
| [`install.mjs`](install.mjs) | The **install**: the pack flow started from version zero, **running no migrations** — the vendored content is already the newest shape, and a record assumes the shapes its own era produced, which an empty repo is not. It stamps the latest version directly, and refuses a pack the repo already has a version for. |
| [`terminals.mjs`](terminals.mjs) | The **uniform terminal**: what happens to an update's PR, given what a flow returned. One function for every flow, so no shell re-decides it. |

The **skew guard** — which mechanism serves a repo while baselining and these flows
both exist — lives in [`engine/served-by.mjs`](../engine/served-by.mjs) rather than
here, because baselining's worker runs from a member's vendored mount and must read
the same definition these flows do.

## The custom update — the one named lane out of the engine flow

The engine flow cannot write `.github/workflows/`: the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may
not push there, and GitHub refuses the **whole ref**, so a workflow file left in the
commit fails the entire update and everything riding it. Ordinary workflow churn is
therefore the pack flow's (owner decision 2) — the scheduler workflow's content is a
function of the task set, so pack changes are what rewrite it.

That leaves one residue: the rare **engine** change that must touch a workflow file
anyway. It ships as a **custom update** — an explicitly named, separately credentialed
operation, run by an MCP-credentialed session or a human, never by the engine flow:

1. The engine release lands normally, *without* the workflow change.
2. The custom update is named in that release's `engine/RELEASES.md` row — which repos
   it must reach, and what it does to each.
3. It runs under a credential that can write workflows, one repo at a time, and the
   row is updated when the fleet is through.

**Naming it is the point.** The lane exists so that "the engine needed a workflow
change" is a visible, credentialed operation with a written trail, rather than an
invisible agentic side door that quietly grows into a general escape hatch. It is for
**workflow files only** — never for a contract change that could not be expressed
mechanically. Those keep backward compatibility or wait (DESIGN §2.3), and the
pressure to route one through here is exactly what the name makes reviewable.

A runner here **judges everything before it writes anything**: a refused update leaves the repo
running exactly what it was running, which is the same transactional contract the vendor writer
keeps. Where it cannot proceed it returns a `needs-human` outcome naming what a person has to do —
it never half-applies, and it never quietly skips the step it could not take.

These run **from a canon checkout against a target repo**, like vendoring: updating is done *on* a
project, never *by* it.

content.text:
## Where it actually lives

It is **a pack task — `core`'s** — but the machinery it drives is split across three lanes:

| Piece | Home | Lane |
|---|---|---|
| Task declaration + agent brief | [`packs/core/tasks/update/task.mjs`](packs/core/tasks/update/task.mjs), [`task.md`](packs/core/tasks/update/task.md) | pack (`core`), vendored, version-gated |
| The runner (clone / branch / PR / terminal) | [`packs/core/tasks/update/worker.mjs`](packs/core/tasks/update/worker.mjs) | pack (`core`) |
| The flows themselves | [`updates/engine-update.mjs`](updates/engine-update.mjs), [`pack-update.mjs`](updates/pack-update.mjs), [`install.mjs`](updates/install.mjs), [`terminals.mjs`](updates/terminals.mjs) | **canon-internal, never vendored** — the worker clones canon fresh and runs *that* copy |
| The skew guard / mechanism vocabulary | [`engine/served-by.mjs`](engine/served-by.mjs) | engine, vendored |

So no member ever executes `updates/*` from its own mount; what a member carries is the `core` task plus the engine helpers the worker imports (`served-by.mjs`, `scheduler/land-pr.mjs`).

## Can it move to a `claudinite-updates` pack?

Mechanically yes, and it would be a mistake as an **opt-in** pack. Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. **Bootstrap circularity with no recovery.** Pack delivery is version-gated per pack and is performed *by this task*. A member that does not already declare the pack has nothing that can deliver it — the only routes in are a migration record or a forced `fleet-baseline` dispatch. `core` escapes this by being `seededByDefault`, `requires`d by `basics`, and declared into pre-existing members by `migrations/2026-08-14-core-seed`. A new pack would need exactly that same triple, at which point it is `core` under another name.
2. **The failure is silent and total.** An undeclared pack contributes nothing — no prose, no checks, no tasks. A member that missed the declaration simply stops converging its mount; every other capability then decays behind it, and the drift looks like a stale stamp rather than a missing pack.
3. **Nothing gets cleaner.** The worker already reaches into `engine/served-by.mjs` and `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`, and pack independence forbids one pack importing another's code — a new pack would hold the identical imports. And `core`'s own `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` explicitly claims *"the self-refresh update"* as its territory, so today's placement is the declared one, not an accident.

The real cost of moving is a fleet-wide declaration change plus a migration record, bought for a relabel.

**If the actual itch is that `core` is broad** (rules index + conformance workflow + task contract + adoption + update), the cheaper fix is not a new pack but co-location/docs: the versioned-updates mechanism is currently spread over `packs/core/tasks/update/`, `updates/`, `engine/served-by.mjs` and [`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md`](docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md), and that scatter — not the pack boundary — is what makes it hard to find.

> ⚠️ No changes made — this was a placement question. My recommendation is to leave `update` in `core`; say the word if you want me to open an issue for the mechanism's scatter across `updates/` / `engine/` / `packs/core/` instead.

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `core-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`core-declared`) |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| Writing or changing a scheduled task | high | correctness | prose: 26 words + checks (`task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`) |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-matches-folder` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-prework-env` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-phase-discipline` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |

What goes wrong when one fires:

- `core-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-checks.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` [barrier](../barriers/README.md) edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
==RULES==

content.text:
## The pack you're describing already exists — it's `core`

Put `update` + `adopt-pack` + `adopt-claudinite` in one pack and you have reassembled [`packs/core`](packs/core) almost exactly. Its current contents:

| | |
|---|---|
| Skills | [`adopt-claudinite`](packs/core/skills/adopt-claudinite), [`adopt-pack`](packs/core/skills/adopt-pack) |
| Tasks | [`update`](packs/core/tasks/update), [`adopt-requested-packs`](packs/core/tasks/adopt-requested-packs) |
| Member-status checks | `core-declared`, `rules-index-current`, `claudinite-isolation`, `conformance-workflow`, `conformance-work-scope`, `scheduler-workflow-shape` |
| Task-authoring contract | [`scheduled-tasks.md`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) + `task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`, `task-phase-discipline` |

And [`pack.mjs:29`](packs/core/pack.mjs) already declares that territory verbatim: *"using Claudinite itself — the vendored mount, the pack declaration, bootstrapping, adopting packs, the self-refresh update"*. So the grouping you're proposing is the one that's in place; what's left is a naming question and one genuine misfit.

## The one thing in `core` that isn't lifecycle

The **scheduled-task authoring contract** — 273 lines of `scheduled-tasks.md` plus four checks — answers "how do I write a task", not "is Claudinite working in this repo". It's also the only part of `core` that's genuinely opt-in-able: those checks are relevance-first (inert unless the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`), and in practice only the canon and Shepherd author tasks. That's a real split; `update`/`adopt-*` is not.

## What a rename would cost

There is **no pack-id alias mechanism** — `engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs` has legacy handling for *paths* (`local_packs/`), nothing for ids. `core` is spelled in every member's `.claudinite-checks.json`, in [`basics/pack.mjs:37`](packs/basics/pack.mjs) `requires`, in [`grow_with_claudinite/pack.mjs:89`](packs/grow_with_claudinite/pack.mjs), and in the [`core-seed`](packs/core/migrations/2026-08-14-core-seed) record. A straight rename hits the #1004 class head-on: for one cycle a member's declaration names a pack the canon no longer ships, the mount self-test fails, the converge refuses to land — and the member can no longer receive the fix. It needs an alias in the loader shipped a full release ahead of the rename, then a record rewriting declarations, then retiring the alias by reading the field. Three cycles for a better noun.

Which of these do you want?

options.label: Leave it (Recommended)
options.description: No change. `core` is already the pack you described, and its ruleRoutingGuidance names that territory. I'd widen the guidance wording if it reads too narrowly, nothing more.

options.label: Split out the task contract
options.description: Move scheduled-tasks.md + task-declaration-shape / -matches-folder / task-prework-env / task-phase-discipline into a new opt-in pack (e.g. `scheduled-tasks`), declared by the canon and Shepherd. `core` keeps update + adopt-* + the member-status checks. Safe: those checks are relevance-first, and nothing bootstraps through them.

options.label: Rename core
options.description: Rename the pack (e.g. `claudinite-lifecycle`). Requires building a pack-id alias in the loader, shipping it a release ahead, then a migration record rewriting every member's declaration, then retiring the alias. Three cycles, fleet-wide, buys naming only.

options.label: Split AND rename
options.description: Both of the above: carve the task contract out, then rename the remainder. Largest change; the rename's two-release alias dance still applies.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.

## The pack you're describing already exists — it's `core`

Everything you'd put in a `claudinite-updates`/`claudinite-lifecycle` pack is already there, together:

| In `core` today | |
|---|---|
| Skills | [`adopt-claudinite`](packs/core/skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md), [`adopt-pack`](packs/core/skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) |
| Tasks | [`update`](packs/core/tasks/update/task.mjs), [`adopt-requested-packs`](packs/core/tasks/adopt-requested-packs/task.mjs) |
| Checks | `core-declared`, `rules-index-current`, `claudinite-isolation`, `conformance-workflow`, `conformance-work-scope`, `scheduler-workflow-shape` |
| Migration | [`2026-08-14-core-seed`](packs/core/migrations/2026-08-14-core-seed/migration.mjs) — declares the pack into every pre-existing member |

Its [`ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs`](packs/core/pack.mjs) already reads *"the vendored mount, the pack declaration, bootstrapping, adopting packs, the self-refresh update"* — the exact bundle you just described. So the proposal isn't "create a pack", it's **"rename `core`"**, and that has a real price:

- `core` is the public id spelled in every member's `.claudinite-checks.json`. A rename is a fleet-wide migration record plus a legacy-id acceptance window in `normalizeManifest` — otherwise a member still declaring `core` silently runs **fewer checks** rather than failing.
- Three in-tree declarers move with it: `basics.requires`, `grow_with_claudinite.requires`, and the `core-seed` record's own `declarePacks`.
- It buys naming only. No capability changes.

## The one thing in `core` that genuinely doesn't fit

Not the update/adopt trio — those cohere. The outsider is the **scheduled-task authoring contract**: [`scheduled-tasks.md`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) (273 lines) plus `task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`, `task-phase-discipline`. Those answer *"how do I write a task"*, not *"is Claudinite working in this repo"* — which is what `core`'s README says every one of its checks is for.

That half is also the only half that's honestly opt-in-able: the checks are relevance-first (inert unless the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`), so a repo that never authors tasks loses nothing. In practice that's the canon and Shepherd declaring it, and nobody else.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

content.text:
Claudinite loaded, 9 packs, 44 checks, 13,000 rule tokens, 21 available skills, 420 personal preference tokens.

Popup dismissed — holding, no changes made. Here's what I found, for when you want to pick it up.

## The bundle you're describing already exists — it's `core`

[`packs/core/`](packs/core/) holds exactly those three things and nothing much else:

| | |
|---|---|
| Skills | [`adopt-claudinite`](packs/core/skills/adopt-claudinite/), [`adopt-pack`](packs/core/skills/adopt-pack/) |
| Tasks | [`update`](packs/core/tasks/update/), [`adopt-requested-packs`](packs/core/tasks/adopt-requested-packs/) |
| Checks | `core-declared`, `rules-index-current`, `claudinite-isolation`, `conformance-workflow`, `conformance-work-scope`, `scheduler-workflow-shape` |
| Plus | [`scheduled-tasks.md`](packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) + `task-declaration-shape` / `task-declaration-matches-folder` / `task-prework-env` / `task-phase-discipline` |

Its own [`README.md`](packs/core/README.md) opens with *"the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to"* — your bundle, verbatim, plus that last clause.

So the question isn't "make a pack for these" — it's whether `core` should shed the one thing that isn't member-lifecycle (the scheduled-task authoring contract), and whether the name should change.

## The two real options

**Split out the task contract.** `scheduled-tasks.md` and the four `task-*` checks answer *"is this task written correctly"*, not *"is Claudinite working in this repo"* — which is the sentence `core`'s README uses to justify every other check in it. They're already relevance-first (inert unless the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`), and in practice only this repo and Shepherd author tasks. That makes it a genuinely opt-in-able pack, unlike the update/adopt half.

**Rename `core`.** Costs a fleet-wide id change: a migration record, a legacy-id acceptance window in `normalizeManifest` (a stale declaration must not degrade to fewer checks running), plus three in-tree references — `packs/basics/pack.mjs:37`, `packs/grow_with_claudinite/pack.mjs:89`, `packs/core/migrations/2026-08-14-core-seed/migration.mjs:30`. Buys naming only.

One constraint holds either way, and it's the same one from before: whatever pack ends up holding `update` must stay **mandatory** — `seededByDefault`, `requires`d by `basics`, seeded by a record. An opt-in pack containing the update task can never be delivered to a member that doesn't already have it, because that task *is* the delivery mechanism.

> ⚠️ Still open: nothing changed. Tell me which of the two (or neither) and I'll open the issue and do it.

input.title: Rename core → claudinite-lifecycle, grow_with_claudinite → claudinite-growth, and move the scheduled-task contract between them
input.body:
Owner decision. Three moves, landed together:

1. **Rename `core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`.** The pack owns the member's Claudinite lifecycle — the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption, the self-refresh update — and `core` says none of that.
2. **Move the scheduled-task authoring contract out of it** — `scheduled-tasks.md` plus `task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`, `task-phase-discipline` — into the growth pack. Those four answer *"is this task written correctly"*, not *"is Claudinite working in this repo"*, which is the sentence the pack's README uses to justify every other check in it.
3. **Rename `grow_with_claudinite` → `claudinite-growth`** — kebab-case like every other pack (the underscore spelling is the grandfathered one), and named for the surface rather than the slogan.

## The hazard that shapes the design

Pack activation matches the declared id **literally**. A member whose `.claudinite-checks.json` says `core` while its mount ships `claudinite-lifecycle` loses the pack entirely — and that pack holds the `update` task, so the member could never receive the fix that would repair it. Same failure class as #1004: a green run, an unmoved stamp, and a mount that can no longer converge.

So the rename cannot be carried by a declaration rewrite alone. It needs **loader-level legacy-id tolerance**: `core` and `grow_with_claudinite` resolve to the renamed packs, in both directions of skew, for as long as any member's declaration or stamp carries the old spelling.

## Delivery

- **Legacy alias map** in the pack loader — one place, mapping every legacy spelling *straight to today's*, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in a single pass.
- **`packVersions` decode** must map the old keys too, or the renamed pack reads as version-absent and the install flow re-stamps it at latest having run no records.
- **An engine migration record** (not a pack record — a pack record lives under the directory the rename removes) to rewrite the declaration and move the stale mount directory. The engine flow runs before the pack flow in the same converge, so a member lands both halves in one cycle.
- **`usage.GENERATED.json`** holds rows keyed by the old pack spelling — the decode side renames them, or the next encode writes those historical counts as `null`.

## Retirement

The aliases come out when no member's declaration or stamp carries an old spelling — read off the fleet, not off a calendar.

The test is `isDormant`, re-exported from the engine, so the sweep and the member's own scheduler cannot disagree.

content.content:
# claudinite-growth

Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.

This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.

Its scheduled work is five tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:

| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |

- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` [barrier](../barriers/README.md) edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.

- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong.

content.text: All green; the only remaining blocker is the release gate demanding a canary run. Rebasing onto the moved `main` first:

input.command:
cd /home/user/Claudinite; git add -A && git -c user.email=[REDACTED:env:CLAUDE_CODE_USER_EMAIL] -c user.name=Claude commit -q -m "Rename core → claudinite-lifecycle and grow_with_claudinite → claudinite-growth

The scheduled-task authoring contract moves with the rename: scheduled-tasks.md
and its four checks judge whether a task is WRITTEN correctly, which is authoring,
not whether Claudinite is working in the repo — so they land in the growth pack
beside the rest of the authoring surface, and the lifecycle pack keeps only the
rules that answer for a member's own Claudinite status.

Activation matches a declared id literally, so the rename's real hazard is a
member whose declaration and mount disagree: it does not get a degraded pack, it
gets none — and for the pack carrying \`update\` that is unrecoverable, because the
machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing.
engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs closes every such window by resolving both
spellings at the loader, on the declared id, the stamped packVersions key, a work
item's stored title, and a mounted pack.mjs still announcing its old id. The

input.title: Rename core → claudinite-lifecycle, grow_with_claudinite → claudinite-growth, and move the scheduled-task contract between them
input.head: claude/update-task-architecture-yseb8o
input.body:
Closes #1022.

Three moves, landed together because the third only makes sense once the first two have names to move between.

## What changed

- **`core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`.** The pack owns a member's Claudinite *status* — the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption, the self-refresh update — and `core` said none of that.
- **`grow_with_claudinite` → `claudinite-growth`**, kebab-case like every other pack (the underscore spelling was the grandfathered one).
- **The scheduled-task authoring contract moves** — `scheduled-tasks.md`, `task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`, `task-phase-discipline`, and the one prose rule that points at the doc — from the first pack to the second. Those five ask whether a task is *written* correctly, which is authoring; every check left behind asks whether Claudinite is *working* in this repo, which is the sentence that pack's README already used to justify all of them.

`claudinite-growth` gains a `RULES.md` for the one rule that came with the contract, so the net prose a session loads is unchanged — it moved, it did not grow.

## The hazard, and what actually handles it

Pack activation matches a declared id **literally**. A member whose `.claudinite-checks.json` says `core` while its mount ships `claudinite-lifecycle` does not get a degraded pack — it gets **none**, and that pack carries the `update` task, so the machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing. Same class as #1004: a green run, an unmoved stamp, and no route back in.

A declaration rewrite alone cannot close that, because the rewrite is one half of a two-half converge and any ordering leaves a window. So the load-bearing piece is `engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs` — one map, every legacy spelling straight to today's, applied at **four** seams where a pack id is read:

| Seam | Why it is a seam |
|---|---|
| `packEntryId` — the declared id | the entry a member wrote before the rename |
| `canonicalPackVersions` — the stamped `packVersions` key | a version under an old key reads as *never installed*, so the install flow re-stamps it at latest having run **no** records in its gap |
| `parseWorkItemTitle` — a work item's `<pack>/<task>` | the title sits on an open issue that outlives any converge; read literally the tick files a second item and orphans the first |
| `discoverPacks` — a mounted `pack.mjs`'s own id | the record moves a member's mount *directory*, but the tree inside is only replaced once the canon ships a version above the one that repo has |

That fourth one is why both renamed packs are bumped past the versions `main` carries: without the bump a member's stamp already satisfies the target, the tree is never replaced, and the mount holds a `pack.mjs` still announcing `core` under a directory named `claudinite-lifecycle`.

Local packs are exempt at every seam — that namespace belongs to the repo, so `local/core` stays `core`.

## The migration record

`engine/migrations/2026-08-19-pack-renames/` — an **engine** record, not a pack one, because a pack record lives under `packs/<id>/migrations/`, which is precisely the directory this change renames. The engine flow also runs before the pack flow in one converge, which is the order this needs: the declaration converges first, the pack flow then reads it and vendors the renamed trees in the same run.

It does two things — moves the stale mount directories (via `aliases`, which fires because the canonical path does not exist yet at that point in the flow), and rewrites the declaration.

The rewrite patterns are deliberately **narrow**. `core` is an ordinary word and an ordinary directory name; a pattern loose enough to catch every spelling also rewrites a member's own `{ "from": "core", "to": "ui/*" }` barrier rule and silently unhooks it. Each pattern can only match a `packVersions` key, an entry object's `id`, or an element of the `packs` array itself. What that misses stays readable anyway via the tolerance above — a trade this record can make and one without that tolerance behind it could not. Both halves are pinned by a test, and the loose-pattern regression was watched failing before the narrow one went in.

## Other consequences

- `core-declared` → `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`. The id named the pack, so it could not survive the rename. Worth flagging: check ids appear in members' `accept` lists, and no alias facility exists for them — this one is blocking-critical and not meaningfully waivable, but it is a real vocabulary change.
- Three test fixtures copied `engine/pack_loader/` file-by-file and broke fail-soft on a new sibling module — mounting nothing and reporting success. They copy the directory now.
- Two reviewed barrier exceptions added, plus `engine/migrations` as a structural carve-out — which the repo's own barriers `goals` text already said it wanted ("migrations/ is deliberately NOT core here"). The one finding on `pattern-rules.mjs` was fixed by deleting the flagged phrase rather than waiving it: a generic engine comment was using a pack name as an example.
- Historical rows in `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` keep the old spelling. They are a per-day record of what ran under the name it had.

## Verification

- Full suite: **2132 passing, 0 failing** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking**.
- `check_the_work`: **1 blocking**, below.
- New assertions were each watched failing first — the legacy-id map, the mounted-stale-id path, and the migration record's narrow patterns.

## The one thing still open

`check_the_work` blocks on `engine-release-record`: **ENGINE_VERSION 5 has no canary rehearsal run.** The bump is not optional — it is what puts the record in every member's gap — so the release gate is correctly refusing until the canary has qualified this tree. Dispatching `canary-rehearsal.yml` against this branch runs a real converge against the canary repo under `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`, which is a world-reaching action, so I have left it for you rather than firing it. Once it passes, its run id replaces `not yet` in the version 5 row.

---

Owner decision. Three moves, landed together in #1029:

1. **Rename `core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`.** The pack owns the member's Claudinite lifecycle — the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption, the self-refresh update — and `core` says none of that.
2. **Move the scheduled-task authoring contract out of it** — `scheduled-tasks.md` plus `task-declaration-shape`, `task-declaration-matches-folder`, `task-prework-env`, `task-phase-discipline` — into the growth pack. Those four answer *"is this task written correctly"*, not *"is Claudinite working in this repo"*, which is the sentence the pack's README uses to justify every other check in it.
3. **Rename `grow_with_claudinite` → `claudinite-growth`** — kebab-case like every other pack (the underscore spelling is the grandfathered one), and named for the surface rather than the slogan.

## The hazard that shapes the design

Pack activation matches the declared id **literally**. A member whose `.claudinite-checks.json` says `core` while its mount ships `claudinite-lifecycle` loses the pack entirely — and that pack holds the `update` task, so the member could never receive the fix that would repair it. Same failure class as #1004: a green run, an unmoved stamp, and a mount that can no longer converge.

So the rename cannot be carried by a declaration rewrite alone. It needs **loader-level legacy-id tolerance**: `core` and `grow_with_claudinite` resolve to the renamed packs, in both directions of skew, for as long as any member's declaration or stamp carries the old spelling.

## Delivery — as built

Four seams read a pack id, and all four canonicalize through one map (`engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs`):

- the **declared id** (`packEntryId`);
- the **stamped `packVersions` key** — a version under an old key reads as *never installed*, so the install flow re-stamps it at latest having run no records in its gap;
- a **work item's stored title** (`parseWorkItemTitle`) — it sits on an open issue that outlives any converge;
- a **mounted `pack.mjs`'s own id** (`discoverPacks`) — the record moves the mount *directory*, but the tree inside is replaced only once the canon ships a version above the one that repo has. Both renamed packs are therefore bumped past `main`'s versions.

Local packs are exempt at every seam.

**An engine migration record** (`2026-08-19-pack-renames`) moves the stale mount directories and rewrites the declaration — engine rather than pack, because a pack record lives under the directory the rename removes, and because the engine flow runs first in a converge. `core-declared` became `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — the id named the pack, so it could not survive.

**`usage.GENERATED.json`** keeps its historical rows under the old spelling: they record what ran under the name it had.

## Retirement

The aliases come out when no member's declaration or stamp carries an old spelling — read off the fleet, not off a calendar.

## Open

ENGINE_VERSION 5 needs a canary rehearsal run before #1029 can merge; the bump is what puts the record in every member's gap, so the release gate is correctly holding. Dispatching it is a world-reaching action against the canary repo and is left to the owner.

On the second finding: I had deferred the canary rehearsal as world-reaching, but that reading was wrong. content.content:
# The LIVE CANARY (#593 phase 3) — the required final step of any core change.
#
# The fixture rehearsal (packs-tests/rehearsal/) is the fast gate: hermetic,
# seconds, on every PR. It has one honest weakness — a fixture only tests what
# someone remembered to model. This is the other half: a REAL repo, really
# adopting Claudinite, really running its own scheduler, converged against this
# canon ref and asked whether it still works.
#
# WHY IT IS A SEPARATE WORKFLOW. It takes minutes, needs a cross-repo token, and
# mutates another repository's working tree. A gate with those properties cannot
# run on every push without becoming something people route around. So: manual
# dispatch, plus automatic on merge to main — the post-merge smoke test, which
# the owner's own framing settles as "still much much better than not knowing".
#
# WHERE THE CANARY IS NAMED. In `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `local/claudinite`
# pack entry's `config.canaryRepo` — the same tracked pack-entry config mechanism
# the sheepdog pack uses for its fleet scope. NOT a GitHub repository variable: the
# binding between this canon and its canary is a fact about the project, and a
# repository variable is invisible in the tree, absent from every diff, and cannot
# be reviewed alongside the workflow that acts on it. A reader of this repo should
# be able to see which repo CI is about to rewrite.
#
# WHY A DEDICATED REPO, NOT A REAL PROJECT. A rehearsal rewrites the mount and
# can leave a failed converge behind. Pointing that at EdFringeNow means a bad
# canon commit leaves a real project dirty at the exact moment attention is
# elsewhere. The canary is disposable by construction; that is its whole value.
#
# WHAT PROTECTS THE CANARY ITSELF: the worker's rehearsal mode
# (CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF) converges, reports, and then RESTORES the working tree —
# no commit, no branch, no PR, and above all no stamp. Stamping a branch head
# would leave the canary `ref-not-on-trunk`, which vendoring's #328 anti-rewind
# guard then refuses to converge over: a rehearsal that wedges its own canary.
name: Canary rehearsal

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Canon ref to rehearse (blank = this workflow's own ref)"
        required: false

The scheduled-task authoring contract moves with the rename: scheduled-tasks.md
and its four checks judge whether a task is WRITTEN correctly, which is authoring,
not whether Claudinite is working in the repo — so they land in the growth pack
beside the rest of the authoring surface, and the lifecycle pack keeps only the
rules that answer for a member's own Claudinite status.

Activation matches a declared id literally, so the rename's real hazard is a
member whose declaration and mount disagree: it does not get a degraded pack, it
gets none — and for the pack carrying `update` that is unrecoverable, because the
machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing.
engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs closes every such window by resolving both
spellings at the loader, on the declared id, the stamped packVersions key, a work
item's stored title, and a mounted pack.mjs still announcing its old id. The
migration record then converges the declaration and moves the mount directories,
so the tolerance can one day be retired — but nothing depends on it having run.

The scheduled-task authoring contract moves with the rename: scheduled-tasks.md
and its four checks judge whether a task is WRITTEN correctly, which is authoring,
not whether Claudinite is working in the repo — so they land in the growth pack
beside the rest of the authoring surface, and the lifecycle pack keeps only the
rules that answer for a member's own Claudinite status.

Activation matches a declared id literally, so the rename's real hazard is a
member whose declaration and mount disagree: it does not get a degraded pack, it
gets none — and for the pack carrying `update` that is unrecoverable, because the
machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing.
engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs closes every such window by resolving both
spellings at the loader, on the declared id, the stamped packVersions key, a work
item's stored title, and a mounted pack.mjs still announcing its old id. The
migration record then converges the declaration and moves the mount directories,
so the tolerance can one day be retired — but nothing depends on it having run.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `claudinite-growth` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

core → claudinite-lifecycle and grow_with_claudinite → claudinite-growth

The scheduled-task authoring contract moves with the rename: scheduled-tasks.md
and its four checks judge whether a task is WRITTEN correctly, which is authoring,
not whether Claudinite is working in the repo — so they land in the growth pack
beside the rest of the authoring surface, and the lifecycle pack keeps only the
rules that answer for a member's own Claudinite status.

Activation matches a declared id literally, so the rename's real hazard is a
member whose declaration and mount disagree: it does not get a degraded pack, it
gets none — and for the pack carrying `update` that is unrecoverable, because the
machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing.
engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs closes every such window by resolving both
spellings at the loader, on the declared id, the stamped packVersions key, a work
item's stored title, and a mounted pack.mjs still announcing its old id. The
migration record then converges the declaration and moves the mount directories,
so the tolerance can one day be retired — but nothing depends on it having run.

core → claudinite-lifecycle and grow_with_claudinite → claudinite-growth

The scheduled-task authoring contract moves with the rename: scheduled-tasks.md
and its four checks judge whether a task is WRITTEN correctly, which is authoring,
not whether Claudinite is working in the repo — so they land in the growth pack
beside the rest of the authoring surface, and the lifecycle pack keeps only the
rules that answer for a member's own Claudinite status.

Activation matches a declared id literally, so the rename's real hazard is a
member whose declaration and mount disagree: it does not get a degraded pack, it
gets none — and for the pack carrying `update` that is unrecoverable, because the
machinery that would deliver the repair is the machinery that went missing.
engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs closes every such window by resolving both
spellings at the loader, on the declared id, the stamped packVersions key, a work
item's stored title, and a mounted pack.mjs still announcing its old id. The
migration record then converges the declaration and moves the mount directories,
so the tolerance can one day be retired — but nothing depends on it having run.

Answering your question, since it's now materially different from an hour ago:

**Yes — there was, and it wasn't cosmetic.** `main` moved twice while the first canary ran, and one of those commits ([#1013](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1013)) renamed the deterministic task phase `prework` → `code-work` — landing in the exact files this change relocates. The rebase produced 21 conflicted paths, including a genuine two-sided rename: `task-prework-env` became `task-code-work-env` on main while this branch was moving it into the growth pack.

Resolved by taking **main's content at this branch's paths** — the contract had to arrive in `claudinite-growth` spelled the way main spells it.
